top_choice_rationale: P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits the achievement on the clearest attribution and best identification in the pool: design-based local-labour-market evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand and regional adjustment. The core papers are a decade or more old and have been replicated across countries and stress-tested on shift-share inference. The remaining debate is over magnitude and persistence, not existence. Dorn is a lead co-author of the China-shock papers and also bridges to the polarisation work with Autor. The cap on three names should not exclude him when the citation is scoped to this evidence. Katz's distinct wage-structure and skill-premium work is mature, but his best-known education-technology work with Goldin overlaps the 2023 prize, and the skill-premium framework has uncredited co-originators. Scoping the citation to import competition and labour-demand adjustment avoids that overlap and does not claim origination of the task framework. P001 is a close second and acceptable on the merits, since it rests on the same evidence base but carries the Katz credit problem. A prize now is better than none given the maturity and replication record, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz is apparent from my profile. Disclosed without adjudication: I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a Swedish party leader and former prime minister (a public fact, with no evidence it bears on any candidate). I have co-authored with Hassler (chair) and Ellingsen. My field of industrial organisation and trade is close to B009 and B034, which are not in the proposal slate.
